At Urbina Bay, you walk over land that was once beneath the sea. In 1954, part of Isabela's coastline rose, leaving marine deposits on dry ground. Along the shore, you can see traces of this event and imagine how quickly a familiar ocean landscape can change.

Urbina lies at the foot of Alcedo Volcano, between Tagus and Elizabeth bays. The most fascinating part of a walk on land is watching iguanas: large yellowish lizards rest among plants and rocks. Giant tortoises can also be found in the area. Every outing brings different wildlife encounters, and a guide helps spot animals that blend into the ground around them.

A visit to the bay brings geology and wildlife together. After landing, it is a pleasure to walk inland from the sandy shore through the island's dry landscape; entering the water depends on conditions and the itinerary. Urbina suits travelers who want to appreciate the Galápagos in detail and understand why its coastlines continue to change.

The Uros Islands lie on Lake Titicaca near Puno. Their foundations and floors are made from totora reeds, which are also used to build houses and traditional boats. The floating islands are maintained and renewed by hand, so reeds remain an important part of everyday life.

A visit to the Uros offers a glimpse of the close connection between local communities and the lake. Fishing, working with reeds, and handicrafts complement views of the open water and high-altitude shores. A visit to the islands can easily be combined with a stay in Puno and other itineraries around Titicaca.

Urubamba lies in the Sacred Valley of the Incas and retains strong ties to agriculture. Corn, potatoes, and other crops are grown in the surrounding area, where fields lie beside mountain slopes. The town is an interesting part of a living rural valley, where ancient history continues through the everyday work of its residents.

There are hotels and restaurants for travelers exploring the region's heritage sites. Colonial buildings survive in Urubamba itself, while the Qespiwanka complex is linked to the area's agricultural heritage from Inca times. A visit to the town complements sightseeing in Pisac and Ollantaytambo with a walk through a lived-in community and an introduction to the valley's rural surroundings.

Ushuaia is the southernmost city on the planet, located on the shores of the Beagle Channel in the Tierra del Fuego archipelago. The Strait of Magellan separates the archipelago from the South American mainland. In the early sixteenth century, while sailing through the strait that would later bear his name, Magellan saw smoke from numerous fires lit by Indigenous people and named the archipelago Tierra del Fuego, or Land of Fire.

Skiing is very popular here. A scenic cross-country skiing route begins in Ushuaia and crosses the mountains of Paso Garibaldi, with their impenetrable forests, peat bogs, Lakes Fagnano and Escondido, and broad plains where thousands of sheep graze. Various routes offer opportunities to travel mountain roads on foot, on horseback, or by motorcycle, taking in the remarkable beauty of the region.

Tierra del Fuego. To this day, there are no other accounts of how this territory received its name. According to this account, Magellan, the explorer of many previously unknown lands, saw numerous lights on the coast from the deck of his ship and assumed a volcano was erupting. Naturally, he named the coastline “Land of Fire.” In reality, the fires were lit at night along the shore by the local Indigenous population.

Antarctica is approximately 900 km from Ushuaia. In town, it is worth visiting the history museum and the old prison, a place associated with the “horrors of imprisonment.” You can take a helicopter flight over the “end of the world,” join a city tour, or ride the world's “southernmost” train, once used to transport prisoners. Walks along the shores of the Beagle Channel offer chances to see seals, penguins, cormorants, condors, and albatrosses. Tierra del Fuego National Park is home to a wide variety of plant and animal species.
